From Para to Dakar

By: Laura Byrne | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Last week, Joey Evans completed the gruelling 9000km Dakar Rally - a decade after he was told he may never walk again

Unique Selling Point:
Paralysed from the chest down in a motor racing accident ten years ago, Joey Evans was told he might never walk again. But not only did he prove doctors wrong - last week he completed the gruelling 9000km Dakar Rally...the only South African to finish in his category.

Summary:
A testament to human determination, the story of Joey Evans's journey from paraplegic to Dakar finisher is the story of a man who refused to give up on his passion.
A lifelong motor sport enthusiast and competitor, Joey broke two vertebrae in a racing accident in 2007. After months in a wheelchair and painfully learning to walk again, he finally got back on a bike, determined to pursue his dream of completing the legendary Dakar Rally. The journey was far from smooth - another accident in 2014 left him with torn ligaments, fractures and lacerations, unable to ride for 6 months. The R1.5 million Dakar price tag was a further obstacle, and Joey embarked on a months-long fundraising campaign with support from friends, fellow racers and an impressive list of smaller donors who he recognised by printing their names on his bike.
Finally, on 2 January 2017, Joey's dream of reaching the Dakar starting line in Paraguay became a reality - and the hard work really began. 14 days, 9000km, and 12 gruelling stages later, he finished - the only South African in the bike category to do so.
We talk to Joey about his long journey back to racing health, his fight to reach the Dakar, and his experience of this most punishing race - from mechanical failure, to injury, to triumph.

Press Release:


Derek Watts: Brave or just plain crazy? Paralysed in a motorbike accident a decade ago, Joey Evans battled pain and disability to reach the Dakar Rally.

Script:


UPSOUND: Joey Evans (From Para to Dakar): the Dakar for me is just the toughest off road race in the world, it’s the big prize, it’s the number one thing.

LINK 1: Derek Watts: The Dakar’s one of the toughest challenges of any kind in the world, taking riders from extreme desert heat to freezing mountain heights. A test of man and machine where many don’t make it to the finish.

VO1: DEREK WATTS: Veteran biker Darryl Curtis has completed the Dakar twice.

UPSOUND: Darryl Curtis (ASO Liaison Officer, Southern Africa): Mentally it’s one of the hardest things I’ve ever done, to push through the pain.

VO2: DEREK WATTS: For Joey Evans, the road to Dakar has been a decade-long test of body and spirit. From BMXing as a kid, Joey’s lifelong passion for motorsport took off when he bought his first motorbike.

LINK 2: Derek Watts: Joey loved the challenge of off road racing and started moving up the ranks. But a decade ago, at an event in Heidelberg, his life changed in a split second.

VO3: DEREK WATTS: Joey’s wife, Meredith, and their four daughters have travelled his long journey with him.

UPSOUND: Meredith Evans (Joey’s wife): I saw another bike hit him and I just saw him go up in the air. And I was with my sister and I said to her, that’s Joey. And I didn’t say anything else, I just started running. He actually, when he came round – because he was unconscious – he joked, did I win? So I thought then, ah, relief, everything’s fine.

VO4: DEREK WATTS: Far from it. His T8 and T9 vertebrae broken, his spinal cord crushed, Joey was paralysed from the chest down. It seemed his motor sport days were over.

UPSOUND: Joey Evans: You look down at a body that you can’t move, that you don’t even recognise, it’s like this isn’t me, this isn’t who I am.

UPSOUND: Sharne Bailey (Physiotherapist): He was a very very competitive rider before he came off his bike, with dreams and aspirations. When you’ve lost something and you’ve had the fire for something, and it’s then suddenly just stripped and taken away, it’s a big thing.

VO5: DEREK WATTS: But miraculously, after a vertebrae fusion that offered only 10% chance of recovery, Joey was able to walk again – and to dream about getting back on a bike…with the help of physiotherapist Sharne Bailey.

UPSOUND: Sharne Bailey (Physiotherapist): There’s so many factors impacting recovery – where the lesion is, if it’s higher or lower in the spinal cord, how much of the spinal cord’s been affected, and then the third one which is a massive psychological and motivational component. Because there are actually no guarantees.

LINK 3: Derek Watts: The tenacity that Joey showed on the racetrack now had to be applied to rehab, but it was a slow process. Sharne built this mock-up of a motorbike just to help him get his leg over the saddle again, and get used to balancing a heavy bike.

UPSOUND: Joey Evans: The first time I got on a bike, I kind of got my leg over and I fell right over with the bike on top of me. To be on a bike where I could move freely and just ride and have the wind just blowing past you and to have this freedom, it was like I had my legs back. It was rehab for the soul.

VO6: DEREK WATTS: And once back on two wheels, the Dakar dream returned.

UPSOUND: Derek Watts: When he said he wanted to do the Dakar, what was your first response?
Meredith Evans: I cried!

UPSOUND: Joey Evans: You’ve got to understand she pushed the wheelchair for me, she helped transfer me from the wheelchair to the bed and in the beginning, she changed nappies for me and all the stuff that’s just the horrible stuff.

UPSOUND: Derek Watts: Do you think he was crazy to take on the Dakar Rally?
[00:06:26] Sharne: Probably. Most definitely. But I just know what type of guy he was and that if he wasn’t going to be able to ride or be on his bike, it would be soul destroying for him.

UPSOUND: Meredith Evans: This is something he’s got to do. It is. It’s going to be hard for us all but we can do it.

VO7: DEREK WATTS: The journey was far from smooth. Another high-speed racing accident in 2014 put Joey out of action for a further 6 months. But as Joey likes to say, he hadn’t come this far to come only this far. Training resumed in earnest.

UPSOUND: Sharne Bailey: So we became more rehab focused and also sort of brainstorming what he would encounter during something like a Dakar.

LINK 4: Derek Watts: Joey may have learnt to walk and to ride again, but now the real work started: qualifying to reach the start line, and most important, raising funds to meet the Dakar price tag.

VO8: DEREK WATTS: Joey funded his R600 000 KTM 450 rally replica bike himself, and the close-knit biking community drew together to raise the R1.1 million shortfall. Seven months later, Joey was on the start line.

UPSOUND: Joey Evans: For a lot of guys it’s been 6 months of hard work or a year of hard work to be there. But I’m standing there on that start line looking back 10 years. To be on that start line for me – I felt like I’d won it already.

VO9: DEREK WATTS: But the ordeal had only just begun. Dakar 2017 took competitors from Paraguay, through Bolivia, to Buenos Aires, Argentina in 12 punishing stages. The field was wide, from competitive professionals to amateurs like Joey – for whom the race is a very different animal.

UPSOUND: Joey Evans: So the track is deeper and more mangled and harder to ride. And you’ve got trucks and cars you’ve got to get out the way for and stop and avoid, and dust. For those guys it’s about times and positions. For me, it’s about I want to live until tonight!

UPSOUND: Darryl Curtis: If I was ever finishing near the back in the Dakar rally, I would never ever race it. And that’s where Joey started off, riding near the back of the field. Because Joey wasn’t there to win this race. He was there to finish this race.

VO10: DEREK WATTS: Joey faced unique challenges. He’s unable to feel heat, cold, or pain below his chest, and he’s unaware of injury until his muscles spasm, as they did when he tore a ligament in his left knee early on.
With an hour or two’s sleep a night, he endured up to 22 hours on the bike day after day…until Stage 11 when disaster struck.

UPSOUND: Joey Evans (Diary Cam): I just had a car go right over my bike. He stopped about 30m off, stands out the car and goes thumbs up. And I’m like, no, help me! And he just gets back in the car and goes. He was this close to killing me and he couldn’t give a stuff. I just don’t know what to do.

UPSOUND: Joey Evans: And then I looked at this bike and I thought, you know what, I’m not going to quit now. I’m going to do whatever I can. I thought if I can drag this bike 10 more metres, I’m going to drag it 10 more metres, and when these guys pick me up, I’m going to be moving.

Derek Watts: What happened? Was there divine intervention?
Joey Evans: I think there was.

UPSOUND: Joey Evans (Diary Cam): I’ve just come across a bike right here, where the rider’s been evacuated, he’s obviously injured. So I’m just going to take everything off his bike that I need, put it onto mine and just continue. It’s freaking insane. But it shows you, you don’t quit. Ever.

VO11: DEREK WATTS: Joey’s fellow South African bikers also fell foul of the landscape. Mechanical issues forced Walter Terblanche out in Stage 4, while a broken leg left David Thomas unable to complete Stage 5.
But after 64 hours in the saddle – fully double Sam Sunderland’s winning time, Joey finished in 94th place.

UPSOUND: Derek Watts: And that finish? How did you feel?
Joey Evans: Ah man, that’s right up there. That’s right up there in my life. I have more than 300 names on my bike of people that helped me to get there. I could feel them all there.

UPSOUND: Darryl Curtis: To finish it is, is everything.

VO12: DEREK WATTS: Three days later he was treated to a hero’s welcome back home.

UPSOUND: Mike Evans (Joey’s brother): I’m just so proud. He’s always been my hero, from when I was – as long as I can remember.

UPSOUND: Paul Vollmer (Biker and fundraiser): Watching Joey scrape it together, knowing that the group of us all had something to do with it – it was like being there yourself.

UPSOUND: Joey Evans (OR Tambo): There’s no words. There’s no words. It’s just fantastic to be here.

VO13: DEREK WATTS: What was it that got Joey through where fitter men fell?

UPSOUND: Darryl Curtis: The perseverance, the tenacity and the friendship that he’s shown to everybody there.

UPSOUND: Meredith Evans: The thing about Joey is just that he never gives up.

UPSOUND Darryl Curtis: This is probably the biggest story of this year’s Dakar.

UPSOUND: Joey Evans: Each day that I get to share another day with my wife and with my family and to be here and to ride my bike and to be alive is just fantastic.


PROMO 1: 15 second (tonight on CB)
VO1: Joey Evans was an up and coming off-road biker until a racing accident changed his life forever.
UPSOUND: Joey [07:02:21] You look down at a body that you can’t move, that you don’t even recognise. It’s like, this isn’t me.
VO2: But his dream of completing the Dakar Rally never died…


PROMO 2: 15 second (tonight on CB)
VO: The Dakar Rally: "A challenge for those who go. A dream for those who stay behind."
UPSOUND: Joey: [07:15:31] It’s the big prize, it’s the number one thing.
Few make it to the start – fewer to the finish. For Joey Evans, the journey started 10 years ago in a wheelchair.


PROMO 3: 10 second (in studio)
Joey Evans’s journey to the Dakar Rally has been one of trial and triumph.
UPSOUND: Joey: [07:17:30] To be on that start line for me – I felt like I’d won already.

And I didn’t say anything else, I just started running. He actually, when he came round – because he was unconscious – he joked, did I win? So I thought then, ah, relief, everything’s fine. VO4: DEREK WATTS: Far from it. His T8 and T9 vertebrae broken, his spinal cord crushed, Joey was paralysed from the chest down. It seemed his motor sport days were over. UPSOUND: Joey Evans: You look down at a body that you can’t move, that you don’t even recognise, it’s like this isn’t me, this isn’t who I am. UPSOUND: Sharne Bailey (Physiotherapist): He was a very very competitive rider before he came off his bike, with dreams and aspirations. When you’ve lost something and you’ve had the fire for something, and it’s then suddenly just stripped and taken away, it’s a big thing. VO5: DEREK WATTS: But miraculously, after a vertebrae fusion that offered only 10% chance of recovery, Joey was able to walk again – and to dream about getting back on a bike…with the help of physiotherapist Sharne Bailey. UPSOUND: Sharne Bailey (Physiotherapist): There’s so many factors impacting recovery – where the lesion is, if it’s higher or lower in the spinal cord, how much of the spinal cord’s been affected, and then the third one which is a massive psychological and motivational component. Because there are actually no guarantees. LINK 3: Derek Watts: The tenacity that Joey showed on the racetrack now had to be applied to rehab, but it was a slow process. Sharne built this mock-up of a motorbike just to help him get his leg over the saddle again, and get used to balancing a heavy bike. UPSOUND: Joey Evans: The first time I got on a bike, I kind of got my leg over and I fell right over with the bike on top of me. To be on a bike where I could move freely and just ride and have the wind just blowing past you and to have this freedom, it was like I had my legs back. It was rehab for the soul. VO6: DEREK WATTS: And once back on two wheels, the Dakar dream returned. UPSOUND: Derek Watts: When he said he wanted to do the Dakar, what was your first response? Meredith Evans: I cried! UPSOUND: Joey Evans: You’ve got to understand she pushed the wheelchair for me, she helped transfer me from the wheelchair to the bed and in the beginning, she changed nappies for me and all the stuff that’s just the horrible stuff. UPSOUND: Derek Watts: Do you think he was crazy to take on the Dakar Rally? [00:06:26] Sharne: Probably. Most definitely. But I just know what type of guy he was and that if he wasn’t going to be able to ride or be on his bike, it would be soul destroying for him. UPSOUND: Meredith Evans: This is something he’s got to do. It is. It’s going to be hard for us all but we can do it. VO7: DEREK WATTS: The journey was far from smooth. Another high-speed racing accident in 2014 put Joey out of action for a further 6 months. But as Joey likes to say, he hadn’t come this far to come only this far. Training resumed in earnest. UPSOUND: Sharne Bailey: So we became more rehab focused and also sort of brainstorming what he would encounter during something like a Dakar. LINK 4: Derek Watts: Joey may have learnt to walk and to ride again, but now the real work started: qualifying to reach the start line, and most important, raising funds to meet the Dakar price tag. VO8: DEREK WATTS: Joey funded his R600 000 KTM 450 rally replica bike himself, and the close-knit biking community drew together to raise the R1.1 million shortfall. Seven months later, Joey was on the start line. UPSOUND: Joey Evans: For a lot of guys it’s been 6 months of hard work or a year of hard work to be there. But I’m standing there on that start line looking back 10 years. To be on that start line for me – I felt like I’d won it already. VO9: DEREK WATTS: But the ordeal had only just begun. Dakar 2017 took competitors from Paraguay, through Bolivia, to Buenos Aires, Argentina in 12 punishing stages. The field was wide, from competitive professionals to amateurs like Joey – for whom the race is a very different animal. UPSOUND: Joey Evans: So the track is deeper and more mangled and harder to ride. And you’ve got trucks and cars you’ve got to get out the way for and stop and avoid, and dust. For those guys it’s about times and positions. For me, it’s about I want to live until tonight! UPSOUND: Darryl Curtis: If I was ever finishing near the back in the Dakar rally, I would never ever race it. And that’s where Joey started off, riding near the back of the field. Because Joey wasn’t there to win this race. He was there to finish this race. VO10: DEREK WATTS: Joey faced unique challenges. He’s unable to feel heat, cold, or pain below his chest, and he’s unaware of injury until his muscles spasm, as they did when he tore a ligament in his left knee early on. With an hour or two’s sleep a night, he endured up to 22 hours on the bike day after day…until Stage 11 when disaster struck. UPSOUND: Joey Evans (Diary Cam): I just had a car go right over my bike. He stopped about 30m off, stands out the car and goes thumbs up. And I’m like, no, help me! And he just gets back in the car and goes. He was this close to killing me and he couldn’t give a stuff. I just don’t know what to do. UPSOUND: Joey Evans: And then I looked at this bike and I thought, you know what, I’m not going to quit now. I’m going to do whatever I can. I thought if I can drag this bike 10 more metres, I’m going to drag it 10 more metres, and when these guys pick me up, I’m going to be moving. Derek Watts: What happened? Was there divine intervention? Joey Evans: I think there was. UPSOUND: Joey Evans (Diary Cam): I’ve just come across a bike right here, where the rider’s been evacuated, he’s obviously injured. So I’m just going to take everything off his bike that I need, put it onto mine and just continue. It’s freaking insane. But it shows you, you don’t quit. Ever. VO11: DEREK WATTS: Joey’s fellow South African bikers also fell foul of the landscape. Mechanical issues forced Walter Terblanche out in Stage 4, while a broken leg left David Thomas unable to complete Stage 5. But after 64 hours in the saddle – fully double Sam Sunderland’s winning time, Joey finished in 94th place. UPSOUND: Derek Watts: And that finish? How did you feel? Joey Evans: Ah man, that’s right up there. That’s right up there in my life. I have more than 300 names on my bike of people that helped me to get there. I could feel them all there. UPSOUND: Darryl Curtis: To finish it is, is everything. VO12: DEREK WATTS: Three days later he was treated to a hero’s welcome back home. UPSOUND: Mike Evans (Joey’s brother): I’m just so proud. He’s always been my hero, from when I was – as long as I can remember. UPSOUND: Paul Vollmer (Biker and fundraiser): Watching Joey scrape it together, knowing that the group of us all had something to do with it – it was like being there yourself. UPSOUND: Joey Evans (OR Tambo): There’s no words. There’s no words. It’s just fantastic to be here. VO13: DEREK WATTS: What was it that got Joey through where fitter men fell? UPSOUND: Darryl Curtis: The perseverance, the tenacity and the friendship that he’s shown to everybody there. UPSOUND: Meredith Evans: The thing about Joey is just that he never gives up. UPSOUND Darryl Curtis: This is probably the biggest story of this year’s Dakar. UPSOUND: Joey Evans: Each day that I get to share another day with my wife and with my family and to be here and to ride my bike and to be alive is just fantastic. PROMO 1: 15 second (tonight on CB) VO1: Joey Evans was an up and coming off-road biker until a racing accident changed his life forever. UPSOUND: Joey [07:02:21] You look down at a body that you can’t move, that you don’t even recognise. It’s like, this isn’t me. VO2: But his dream of completing the Dakar Rally never died… PROMO 2: 15 second (tonight on CB) VO: The Dakar Rally: "A challenge for those who go. A dream for those who stay behind." UPSOUND: Joey: [07:15:31] It’s the big prize, it’s the number one thing. Few make it to the start – fewer to the finish. For Joey Evans, the journey started 10 years ago in a wheelchair. PROMO 3: 10 second (in studio) Joey Evans’s journey to the Dakar Rally has been one of trial and triumph. UPSOUND: Joey: [07:17:30] To be on that start line for me – I felt like I’d won already. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Last week, Joey Evans completed the gruelling 9000km Dakar Rally - a decade after he was told he may never walk again
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Paralysed from the chest down in a motor racing accident ten years ago, Joey Evans was told he might never walk again. But not only did he prove doctors wrong - last week he completed the gruelling 9000km Dakar Rally...the only South African to finish in his category.
metadata.Summary: A testament to human determination, the story of Joey Evans's journey from paraplegic to Dakar finisher is the story of a man who refused to give up on his passion. A lifelong motor sport enthusiast and competitor, Joey broke two vertebrae in a racing accident in 2007. After months in a wheelchair and painfully learning to walk again, he finally got back on a bike, determined to pursue his dream of completing the legendary Dakar Rally. The journey was far from smooth - another accident in 2014 left him with torn ligaments, fractures and lacerations, unable to ride for 6 months. The R1.5 million Dakar price tag was a further obstacle, and Joey embarked on a months-long fundraising campaign with support from friends, fellow racers and an impressive list of smaller donors who he recognised by printing their names on his bike. Finally, on 2 January 2017, Joey's dream of reaching the Dakar starting line in Paraguay became a reality - and the hard work really began. 14 days, 9000km, and 12 gruelling stages later, he finished - the only South African in the bike category to do so. We talk to Joey about his long journey back to racing health, his fight to reach the Dakar, and his experience of this most punishing race - from mechanical failure, to injury, to triumph.
